claims.text: High-entropy alloys exhibit superior simultaneous wear-corrosion resistance compared with conventional alloys.
A multi-principal-element composition enables continuous, self-adaptive regeneration of a protective oxide film during cyclic mechanical abrasion.
The proposed HEA has a uniform single-phase or near-single-phase microstructure with homogeneously distributed oxide-forming elements.
NS4 solution permits formation of a protective passivation oxide on an HEA coating.
Allowing sufficient time between wear events supports passive-film regrowth.
A dynamic multi-element oxide or intermetallic film rapidly forms on the worn surface and replenishes material removed from the protective layer.
Mechanical wear intermittently removes portions of the initial passive film.
The presence of several oxide-forming elements in the HEA drives rapid repassivation of exposed surfaces.
A dynamic equilibrium between passive-film removal and regeneration produces less-than-additive combined degradation relative to separate wear and corrosion.
The HEA will have lower net combined wear-corrosion degradation than the matched conventional alloy.
The HEA will exhibit reduced wear volume loss relative to the conventional alloy.
The HEA will exhibit lower corrosion current density relative to the conventional alloy.
Passive-film electrochemical properties will recover during cyclic wear-corrosion testing.
Less-than-additive degradation is indicative of effective dynamic repassivation.
The conventional baseline derives its wear and corrosion resistance primarily from static passive films and lacks significant repassivation during cyclic wear.
The predicted benefit holds when abrasion rate, electrolyte, temperature, and pH permit oxide-film reformation.
The mechanism can fail when wear removal overwhelms repassivation kinetics or necessary oxide-forming species are absent.
The degree of protection may vary with alloy composition and testing conditions.
